title: Principle and foundation
hook: we are made to praise, reverence and serve God; use things as far as they help

segments.voice: Yesterday, pots and pans: Brother Lawrence at the stove, turning the cake for the love of God. Your line was turn it for love. Which chore did you turn? Day one thousand one hundred thirty-nine.

A Basque soldier is carried home with a shattered leg. Stuck in bed for a long recovery, he asks for adventure stories. The house doesn't have any. What it has is a life of Christ and a book of saints' lives. He reads them, out of boredom, and something in him turns. That's how his own Autobiography tells it. His name is Ignatius of Loyola. Out of what happened next came a small handbook for a guide leading someone through prayer, called the Spiritual Exercises. Today we leave the Carmelites' kitchen and walk into a new room of Christian prayer, the Ignatian way. And it starts with one short paragraph that the whole handbook stands on. Ignatius calls it the principle and foundation.

Here's the paragraph, in plain words. Human beings are created to praise, reverence and serve God our Lord, and so to save their souls. Everything else on the face of the earth is created for us, to help us toward that end. So we should use things as far as they help us toward it, and let go of them as far as they get in the way. That's it. It sounds dry, almost like an engineer wrote it. But look at what it does. It doesn't sort the world into holy things and bad things. Money, a job, a phone, a friendship, an ambition: none of it is the enemy, and none of it is the point. Each one gets the same quiet question. Does it help? The measure is the purpose, not the thing. Paul had asked a similar question about Christian freedom: "All things are lawful unto me, but all things are not expedient." Paul's Greek word for expedient, sympherei, means it's useful, it helps. Plenty is allowed. Not all of it helps. And the opening line matters as much as the rule. Ignatius starts with what we're for. Praise, reverence, service. Revelation puts that same note in the mouths of the elders around God's throne: "Thou art worthy, O Lord, to receive glory and honour and power: for thou hast created all things." Begin there, in Ignatius's way of seeing, and every other choice gets simpler. Not easier, always. But simpler. You're no longer asking what you want. You're asking what helps.
screen: `USE THINGS AS FAR AS THEY HELP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: check one thing with Ignatius's question. Sit and breathe. Bring to mind one thing that takes up real space in your life: an app, a habit, a hobby, a commitment, a possession. Don't judge it yet. Just hold it up and ask: does this help me toward what I'm for? If you pray, you can ask God to show you. If you don't, ask whether it helps you love and serve well. Notice the answer, even if it's mixed. The bell holds the time.
Principle and foundation. The opening of Ignatius's Spiritual Exercises: we're made to praise, reverence and serve God, and we use everything else as far as it helps.
Your line: as far as it helps. Today, before you reach for the thing you reach for without thinking, ask the question once. Does it help? Day one thousand one hundred thirty-nine.

howItsDone: Jesuits and others who make the Spiritual Exercises, in a long retreat or in daily life with a guide, usually begin by praying with the Principle and Foundation, and return to it when making decisions.

fork.setup: you're making the Exercises. a new job offer comes, with more money and less time for the people you love. what's Ignatius's first question?
options: which option helps toward what I'm made for?
fork.reveal: the principle and foundation measures every choice by the purpose: praise, reverence and service of God. use things as far as they help.

original.note: Greek: it is useful, it helps; the word the King James renders expedient in 1 Corinthians 6:12.

trapdoor: what you thought: a principle and foundation is a dull opening paragraph.
what it means: the ground of the Spiritual Exercises: we're made for God, and everything else is used as far as it helps.
what a scholar hears: Ignatius's Spanish is tanto cuanto, as much as: use things as much as they help and leave them as much as they hinder.

notes: Spiritual Exercises §23 paraphrased (Mullan 1914 is pre-1929 but not on the validator's list): 'Man is created to praise, reverence and serve God our Lord, and by this means to save his soul...'. Confirm the paraphrase.
Hook: shattered leg, request for books of chivalry, a life of Christ and saints' lives in the house: from the Autobiography ch. 1. Confirm. No date or place of the battle given.
Trapdoor: 'tanto cuanto' as the Spanish phrase of §23; confirm.
Original: συμφέρει in 1 Corinthians 6:12, gloss 'it is useful, it helps'; confirm accent and pronunciation.
'Not easier, always' is a phrase about choices, not a claim about Christians.
Revelation 4:10–11 attributed to the elders around the throne; confirm.
Editor (2026-10-02): 'Begin there, Ignatius says, and every other choice gets simpler' put words in Ignatius's mouth that §23 doesn't say; reframed as his way of seeing.
Auditor (2026-10-02): §23, Autobiography ch. 1, 1 Corinthians 6:12 and Revelation 4:11 checked; no changes needed.
